Empirical Research Plan  
“Does the CAPM premium show up when macro‐news arrives?”

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Method:  Difference-in-Differences with a continuous treatment  
  •  Time dimension: announcement versus non-announcement days  
  •  Cross-section: ex-ante market beta (continuous or quintiles)

Specification (firm-day level):

    ExcessReturn_it = α_i + γ_t + β₁·Beta_i + β₂·Ann_t 
                      + β₃·(Beta_i × Ann_t) + X_it′δ + ε_it

β₃ is the DiD estimator: the incremental beta-return slope that is present only on announcement days.  

Why appropriate?  
• Announcement dates are fixed ex ante by government agencies/FOMC → timing plausibly exogenous to individual stocks.  
• Beta is predetermined (estimated from the prior 250 trading days), so the cross-section is known before the “treatment” occurs.  
• Combining the two dimensions yields a clean counterfactual: how would a high-beta stock have performed on an otherwise identical day that was not an announcement day?

================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  Ann_t  = 1 if day t contains at least one of: BLS employment, CPI, FOMC statement/decision; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
  All trading days without any of the three macro releases.

Cross-sectional variation  
  Continuous: firm’s rolling‐year CAPM beta (Beta_i).  
  Discrete robustness: beta-quintile portfolios.

Timing  
  Treatment occurs once per day; firms are considered “exposed” on that day.  Betas are held fixed for the whole month (or 20-day window) to avoid look-ahead bias.

================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Exogenous timing of announcements  
     Government agencies set release calendars long before the information is compiled → firm-level shocks do not influence the calendar.

A2.  Parallel trends (common-shock)  
     In the absence of news, the return–beta slope would be the same on announcement and non-announcement days.  Plausible because both sets of days share the same month-of-year, day-of-week, etc., which we will capture with date fixed effects.

A3.  No systematic pre-announcement price drift that differs by beta (no differential anticipation).  We test this with leads of Ann_t.

A4.  Betas are measured with error but the error is classical (uncorrelated with Ann_t); rolling estimation from past returns makes this plausible.

================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1.  Information leakage / anticipation  
     • Remove day −1 and day +1 from the sample.  
     • Include leads/lags of Ann_t to show the interaction slope is zero outside day 0.

T2.  Other clustered information events (earnings seasons, option expiration, month-end effects)  
     • Add dummies for earnings-announcement days and for calendar effects (month-end, option expiration).  
     • Keep date fixed effects when running portfolio-level regressions.

T3.  Heteroskedasticity and cross-firm correlation in returns  
     • Cluster standard errors at the date level (all firms share the same shock).  
     • For portfolio-level regressions, use Newey-West (4 lags).

T4.  Time-varying market price of risk unrelated to announcements (e.g., crises)  
     • Interact Beta_i with a Crisis_t dummy (NBER recessions, 2008 crisis) to show the results are not solely crisis-driven.  
     • Run the model separately in expansions vs. recessions.

================================================================
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# PACKAGES ------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast I/O
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE regressions
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)

# 1. READ DATA --------------------------------------------------
stocks  <- fread("crsp_daily.csv")          # permno, date, ret, beta
ann     <- fread("macro_announcements.csv") # date, emp, cpi, fomc (0/1)

rf      <- fread("rf_daily.csv")            # date, rf
factors <- fread("FamaFrench_factors.csv")  # date, mkt, smb, hml, umd

# 2. MERGE ------------------------------------------------------
dt <- stocks %>%
      left_join(rf,     by = "date") %>%
      mutate(excess = ret - rf) %>%
      left_join(ann %>% mutate(Ann = if_else(emp==1 | cpi==1 | fomc==1,1,0)),
                by = "date") %>%
      left_join(factors, by = "date") %>%
      mutate(beta_q = ntile(beta, 5)) %>%   # quintiles for robustness
      data.table()

# 3. MAIN REGRESSION -------------------------------------------
# firm-day level, date clustered SE
mod <- feols(excess ~ beta*Ann + beta + Ann,
             data = dt,
             fixef = ~permno + date,   # firm and date FE
             cluster = ~date)

etable(mod, se = "cluster")

# 4. ROBUSTNESS: portfolio-day & FF controls -------------------
port <- dt[, .(vwret = weighted.mean(excess, mktcap, na.rm=TRUE)),
           by = .(date, beta_q, Ann)]

rob <- feols(vwret ~ beta_q*Ann + mkt + smb + hml + umd,
             data = port, cluster = ~date)

etable(list(FirmDay = mod, PortDay = rob), se = "cluster")

# 5. ANTICIPATION CHECK (leads/lags) ---------------------------
dt[, Ann_lead1 := shift(Ann, 1, type = "lead"), by = permno]
dt[, Ann_lag1  := shift(Ann, 1, type = "lag"),  by = permno]

leadlag <- feols(excess ~ beta*Ann + beta*Ann_lead1 + beta*Ann_lag1 +
                           beta + Ann + Ann_lead1 + Ann_lag1,
                 data = dt, fixef = ~permno + date, cluster = ~date)
etable(leadlag, se="cluster")
```

================================================================
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts β₃ > 0.  A rough calibration:

• Average daily equity risk premium ≈ 4 bp.  
• Only ~28% of days are announcement days → premium needs to be ≈ 14 bp on those days to recover 4 bp unconditionally.  

Thus I expect β₃ ≈ 0.14% (=14 bp) per unit of beta; e.g., a stock with β=1.5 earns about 7 bp more than a β=0.5 stock on announcement days, while the beta-return slope on non-announcement days is statistically indistinguishable from zero.

================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = weak)
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Exogeneity of treatment timing ............... 0.9  
2. Parallel trends (beta-return slope) .......... 0.7  
3. No anticipation / spillovers ................. 0.6  
4. Accurate measurement of treatment & beta ..... 0.8  
5. Stable unit treatment value (no interference)  0.9  

Overall, the design is strong but rests on the absence of differential anticipation by beta, which must be tested explicitly.
